passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from your arrival date in Madagascar, with at least one blank page for the visa.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required only if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. There is no yellow fever in Madagascar itself.

source.name: Madagascar eVisa — official online visa portal

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked at the border, but medical facilities are basic outside Antananarivo and serious cases require evacuation to Réunion or South Africa — comprehensive coverage with medical evacuation is strongly recommended.

source.name: Madagascar eVisa — official online visa portal

onwardTicket.text: A return or onward ticket is a condition of the tourist visa and airlines routinely check it before boarding.

source.name: Madagascar eVisa — official online visa portal

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; immigration officers rarely ask, but be prepared to show means of support for longer stays.

source.name: Madagascar eVisa — official online visa portal

currencyLimits.text: Foreign currency worth EUR 10,000 or more must be declared on arrival, and Malagasy ariary may only be taken out of the country in small amounts. Confirm current thresholds before travel.

notes: Exporting vanilla, gemstones and precious woods is tightly controlled. Buy from licensed dealers and keep receipts for customs.
It is prohibited to take protected wildlife, corals, seashells or fossils out of Madagascar.

payments.text: Cards work at upmarket hotels and some restaurants in Antananarivo and the main tourist towns, but Madagascar runs on cash. Carry ariary in small notes, and note that ATMs are scarce outside larger towns.

safety.text: Most visits are trouble-free, but political conditions have been volatile since the change of government in late 2025, and robbery and petty crime are risks in Antananarivo and on isolated beaches. Avoid demonstrations, do not walk in cities after dark, and use trusted drivers for long road journeys.

bestTimeToVisit.text: April to October — the cooler, dry season — is best for wildlife, the RN7 route and the beaches; November to March brings heavy rain and cyclone risk, especially on the east coast.

idp.text: Madagascar is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

driving.text: Madagascar is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Madagascar yet.

tips.text: Cyclones regularly strike Madagascar between November and April, especially on the east coast — flights and roads can be cut for days, so monitor forecasts and build slack into any rainy-season itinerary.

Political conditions have been unsettled since the change of government in late 2025. Avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, follow local news and check your government's travel advice before and during your trip.
Change money at banks or official bureaux and carry enough ariary for several days whenever you leave a major town — card payment and ATMs are scarce in rural areas.
Road travel is slow — a few hundred kilometers can take a full day on degraded roads — so most visitors use domestic flights to cover long distances.
Malaria is present year-round in coastal and lowland areas. Take prophylaxis, use repellent and sleep under nets; the central highlands carry lower risk.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Madagascar?
faq.answer: Yes, but it is easy: every nationality can obtain a tourist visa, either on arrival at the airport or online in advance at evisa.mg. Visas come in 15-, 30- and 60-day versions, with the fee depending on length of stay.

faq.question: How much does the Madagascar visa cost?
faq.answer: Approximately EUR 10 for up to 15 days, EUR 35 for 30 days and EUR 40 for 60 days, payable in euros, US dollars or ariary. Tariffs change periodically. Confirm the current amounts on evisa.mg before travel.

faq.question: Should I get the eVisa or a visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Both lead to the same tourist visa. Applying at evisa.mg before travel saves queueing after a long flight, while the visa on arrival remains available to all nationalities at international airports — if you choose it, carry the fee in cash.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Madagascar?
faq.answer: Tourist stays can generally be extended in-country up to a maximum of around 90 days in total, handled by the Ministry of the Interior in Antananarivo. Start well before your visa expires and confirm the current procedure locally — requirements change.

faq.question: Is Madagascar safe to visit?
faq.answer: Most trips are trouble-free, but take petty and opportunistic crime seriously in Antananarivo and on isolated beaches, avoid demonstrations given the unsettled political situation, and plan around the November–April cyclone season. Check your government's travel advice before booking.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit Madagascar?
faq.answer: April to October, in the dry season — cooler weather, passable roads and the best wildlife viewing. July to September adds humpback whale watching off Île Sainte-Marie. November to March is cyclone season, with heavy rain in the north and east.
